analysis.one_liner: Makes community college tuition-free and eliminates tuition at public four-year colleges for working- and middle-class students.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced in April 2021 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have the federal government pay states and tribal colleges to eliminate tuition and fees at community colleges for everyone, and at public four-year colleges for students from families earning up to $125,000. It would roughly double the maximum Pell Grant, let Pell money cover living expenses, make 'Dreamer' students eligible for federal aid, and send large grants to underfunded and minority-serving colleges. It was never taken up by the Senate committee that received it.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, students at community colleges would owe no tuition or fees; students at public four-year and tribal colleges from families earning $125,000 or less would owe none either [S2][S3]. The maximum Pell Grant would rise to $12,990 at public and tribal colleges and could be used for living and non-tuition expenses, not just tuition [S3]. Immigrants brought to the U.S. as children ('Dreamers') would become eligible for federal financial aid for the first time [S2][S3]. Underfunded colleges, historically Black colleges, and other minority-serving institutions would receive grants for advising, counseling, tutoring, and smaller classes [S2][S3]. Colleges would be required to prioritize hiring tenure-track faculty over part-time instructors and to maintain instructional spending [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Provides grants to states covering 75% of the cost of eliminating tuition and fees at community colleges for all students and at public four-year colleges for students whose families earn $125,000 or less, with an income threshold that rises with average wages [S2][S3].
Raises the maximum Pell Grant to $12,990 at public and tribal colleges, extends eligibility from 12 semesters to 7.5 years, and lets students spend grant money on living expenses [S3].
Makes Dreamer students who entered the U.S. before age 16 and completed high school or service eligible for federal financial aid, including Pell Grants [S2][S3].

Authorizes $10 billion a year in equity grants to underfunded and minority-serving colleges for support programs aimed at graduation rates, plus $3 billion for TRIO programs and $736 million for GEAR UP [S2][S3].

Requires participating colleges to maintain instructional spending, staff at least 75% of instruction with tenure-track or tenured faculty within five years, and prioritize converting adjuncts to tenure-track jobs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would fund the program through mandatory appropriations with no dedicated revenue source in the bill, so the cost would fall on general taxpayers through borrowing or other federal revenue [S3]. Participating states would have to cover at least a 25% share of tuition costs and keep their own higher-education spending at 2019-20 levels, requirements that would constrain state budgets in recessions (the bill includes an automatic stabilizer lowering the state share to 10% during high unemployment) [S3]. Tuition revenue at private nonprofit colleges outside the HBCU/MSI carve-out would face new competition from a free public alternative [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates money directly out of the Treasury for fiscal years 2021 through 2030 with no offsetting revenue or spending cuts, so its large and ongoing cost would add to federal deficits unless Congress separately raised taxes or cut other programs [S3].

States must put up at least 25% of the tuition cost and pledge not to cut their own higher-education or need-based aid spending below 2019-20 levels, conditions some states would struggle to meet or would resent as a federal mandate on their budgets [S3].

The $125,000 income cutoff for free four-year tuition covers many households well above the national median, which means a large share of the new spending would go to families that could already pay tuition, and the bill gives no new aid to students at private nonprofit colleges outside the HBCU/MSI carve-out [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: free community college for everyone, free public four-year tuition for most working and middle-class families, a doubled Pell Grant that can cover rent and food, and new aid eligibility for Dreamers. The honest cost side is that the bill required tens of billions in new federal spending every year with no funding mechanism attached, pushed a significant match onto state budgets, and would have shifted enrollment toward public colleges at the expense of private ones. The design also directs new money at families up to $125,000, spreading dollars thinner than a tighter income cap would. On balance it was a major redistribution toward students and away from general federal revenue, and its fate depended entirely on whether Congress was willing to fund it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the College for All Act of 2021 on April 21, 2021, joined by nine Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over federal revenue matters [S5].

No further action appears in the bill's record: the Finance Committee never held a hearing or markup, the full Senate never voted, and the House never considered a companion measure, so the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Institutions that charge tuition — for-profit colleges and private nonprofit universities outside the HBCU/MSI carve-out — kept their enrollment and revenue, and the federal government spent nothing on the program. Students who would have gotten free or cheaper college instead continued to pay tuition and take on debt.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tuition-charging colleges and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 9 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Warren, Padilla, Murphy, Merkley, Markey, Leahy, Blumenthal, and Gillibrand.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its referral.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored the bill or backed its consideration.

against.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
against.role: Senator from West Virginia, key holdout on the Build Back Better reconciliation package
against.what_they_did: Opposed the broader spending package that carried a tuition-free community college proposal, dooming the parallel effort that stood the best chance of enactment.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was an Independent who caucuses with Democrats and all nine cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported it, and no vote was ever held to measure the split further [S4].

industries.note: Federal grants would replace the tuition revenue the bill eliminates, and colleges would be required to maintain instructional spending and hire more tenure-track faculty. Students and public institutions both come out ahead.

The bill would bar institutions that converted from for-profit to nonprofit status from receiving tuition grants for 25 years, and a free public alternative would draw away students who currently borrow federal aid to attend for-profit schools.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit colleges (outside the HBCU/MSI carve-out)
industries.note: Their students would face free public options that the bill does not extend to private institutions outside historically Black and minority-serving schools, putting their enrollment and tuition revenue at risk.
Free tuition and larger Pell Grants that cover living costs would reduce how much students need to borrow, shrinking the loan volume that federal and private loan servicing depends on.
